title: Rishi Sunak Returns to Delhi's Bengali Sweet House for Aloo Tikki and Rasmalai With Sudha Murty
excerpt: In Delhi for the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, the former UK prime minister revisited a favourite Bengali Market institution with his mother-in-law Sudha Murty and Swati Maliwal — for chaat, lassi, laddoos and rasmalai.
body:
• Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak visited Bengali Sweet House in Delhi's Bengali Market with his mother-in-law, Rajya Sabha MP Sudha Murty, and MP Swati Maliwal.
  • The group ate chaat and aloo tikki, drank lassi and tea, and finished with laddoos, gulab jamun and rasmalai — described in the shop's posts as one of Sunak's favourite Indian desserts.
  • Sunak was in Delhi for the Bloomberg New Economy Forum and met Prime Minister Narendra Modi during the trip; the sweet-shop stop was a return visit after a 2025 pre-Diwali trip to the same shop.
  • Bengali Sweet House has traded in Bengali Market since 1937 and counts Sudha Murty as a regular customer.

Chaat first, meetings later

Former British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's Delhi schedule included a global economy forum and a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. It also included aloo tikki. Sunak stopped at Bengali Sweet House in Bengali Market with his mother-in-law, author and Rajya Sabha MP Sudha Murty, and fellow Rajya Sabha MP Swati Maliwal, in a visit captured in photos and videos shared by the shop and by Maliwal, according to Aaj Tak.

The order was unapologetically classic Delhi: chaat, aloo tikki, lassi and tea, followed by the sweet counter — laddoos, gulab jamun and rasmalai. Aaj Tak reported that motichoor laddoos drew a particularly pleased reaction when they were served. Maliwal, whose birthday coincided with the outing, described the afternoon in her social media caption as time spent over Delhi chaat, rasmalai and laddoo with Sunak and Murty, her mentor in Parliament.

"The order was unapologetically classic Delhi: chaat, aloo tikki, lassi and tea, followed by the sweet counter — laddoos, gulab jamun and rasmalai."

A favourite shop, not a first visit

This was a return, not a discovery. Curly Tales reported that Sunak had visited the same shop in 2025 shortly before Diwali, remembered its festive decorations, and spoke then about mithai being central to Diwali for him, including a fondness for kulfi. The CSR Journal noted that Murty herself is a loyal, repeat customer who has visited with her daughter Akshata Murty, Sunak's wife.

That family thread is what gives a snack stop its resonance. Sunak, Britain's first prime minister of Indian heritage, married into one of India's best-known business and philanthropic families. A Delhi chaat outing led by his mother-in-law is, in diaspora terms, the most ordinary kind of family ritual — which is precisely why the images travelled so widely.

The shop behind the photos

Bengali Sweet House has been part of Bengali Market since 1937, after its founders first set up near the Sessions Court on Ferozshah Road in 1936. The idea, carried across nearly nine decades, was simple: serve the street food people already loved in a place where families could sit down comfortably. Its menu still runs from chaat, chole bhature and kachori to thalis and South Indian dishes, with a sweet counter spanning traditional Bengali sweets to sugar-free options.

Its customer list over the decades has included film stars and politicians across parties — a reminder that in Delhi, a good chaat shop is neutral territory. Sunak, Murty and Maliwal are simply its latest well-photographed table.

Why it lands with the diaspora

For Indian families in Britain, the story needs no explanation: a son-in-law being taken for chaat by his mother-in-law, returning to a favourite shop, and lighting up at motichoor laddoos is a scene played out in thousands of households every Diwali season. If you are in Delhi this festive season, the practical takeaway is the address itself — Bengali Sweet House, Bengali Market, near Connaught Place — and the order the table chose: aloo tikki and chaat to start, rasmalai to finish.
